independent.summary: The own-origin allowlist entry is built from `req.get('host')`, which in Express 4 returns the raw `Host` header and never `X-Forwarded-Host` (express/lib/request.js:65-84 only special-cases referer/referrer) — so the inline comment "req.get honours X-Forwarded-Host behind the trusted proxy" is false, and behind a proxy that rewrites Host the allowlist would hold the internal host, 403-ing the API's own OAuth approval POST (/authorize, /bridge/authorize) whenever it is not also CLIENT_ORIGIN. The unit test that claims to cover this (tests/unit/originGuard.test.js, "the own-origin entry follows the forwarded host behind a trusted proxy") replaces `req.get` with its own stub returning the public host, so it asserts the stub rather than Express's behaviour and would stay green either way; `req.hostname` (plus port) is what honours the forwarded host.

grades.reason: `app.use(originGuard)` sits at app.js:96, ahead of every router including `/auth`, and tests/http/originGuard.test.js proves `POST /auth/logout` with `Origin: evil.test` is 403 — there is no per-route mounting to miss (and app.js has no line 191).
`originOf('*')` fails `new URL()` and returns null, so the request falls into the refusal branch; a literal `*` Origin is 403, not a bypass (and no browser sends it).

`POST /auth/register` has no signed-in session to ride, so the guard deliberately does not check it (documented as out of scope in the decision log) — and a bogus Origin on registration grants an attacker nothing.

A test suite must pin the origin it configures and sends; `CLIENT_ORIGIN` in tests/helpers/origin.js is test fixture data, not a deployment setting, and no production value is hardcoded anywhere in the diff.
Same non-issue as finding 4 restated for chat.test.js — a test-local constant that matches what the suite sets in `process.env.CLIENT_ORIGIN` is exactly the intended design.
Same non-issue as findings 4 and 5 restated for composeDraft.test.js; pinning the fixture origin is correct, not a security problem.

The refusal tests do assert the database is untouched (`titled(title)` is null after the 403, and the unsafe-methods test re-reads the entity and asserts it still exists with its original summary after a refused PUT and DELETE).

The very first http test is a JSON `POST /entities` with `Origin: https://evil.test` asserting 403 and no entity written; the "JSON is parsed as it always was" test is a separate regression check, not the origin case.

The missing-Origin/matching-Referer branch is covered in tests/unit/originGuard.test.js and tests/http/originGuard.test.js; passkeys.test.js is not where that behaviour belongs, and its omission is not a defect.

triageGrades.reason: The change adds a session-authentication/CSRF middleware mounted after express-session and rewires auth-related tests, so auth is plainly touched.
No secret is added, read, or logged; the only token in the diff is the existing test fixture `test-mcp-bearer-token` in a test file.
No billing, pricing, or quota code changes — the AI-allowance endpoint is only mentioned as motivation in comments and docs.

The diff performs no destructive operation (no deletes, drops, migrations, or data rewrites) — it only refuses requests — and the cited evidence file server/src/routes/entities.js is not modified by this change at all.
No outbound integration changes; the OAuth/token endpoints touched are this API's own issuers, with only the body parser moved.
No version bump, CI, container, or deploy-manifest change; `.env.example` only documents an optional log-level var and clarifies an existing one.

summary: All nine findings are false positives — three are the same "hardcoded test origin" non-issue repeated, four complain about coverage that the new test files demonstrably contain, and two misstate the code (guard not mounted on /auth/logout; `*` Origin bypass) — and the one real defect, the false X-Forwarded-Host claim and the unit test that stubs it, was missed.
